newsitem.title: USA: GM shows off Delphi results to Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: GM shows off Delphi results to Wall Street.

text.p: General Motors Corp., preparing Wall Street for a future public offering in its Delphi Automotive Systems parts unit, Wednesday released first-ever separate results for Delphi that showed a 42.6 percent decline in 1996 earnings.

GM, which long has combined Delphi results with those of its North American vehicle assembly operations, insisted that the release of Delphi results is not directly related to the possible sale of a 20 percent stake in Delphi, which ranks as the world's largest automotive supplier.

GM announced that it would consider such a transaction involving its combined Delphi and Delco Electronics units in January, when it agreed to sell its Hughes Aircraft defence operations to Raytheon Co. for $9.5 billion.

"Certainly it's consistent with what we would have to do if there were to be public ownership of some portion of Delphi going forward," GM Chief Financial Officer J. Michael Losh told reporters in a conference call, adding that GM planned to release the Delphi results anyway.
"It's really to help people understand the major comnponents of General Motors a bit better than they've been able to heretofore," Losh said added.
The release coincided with a GM presentation to Wall Street auto analysts in Rye, N.Y., on Wednesday. The Delphi results exclude Delco Electronics.

GM said Delphi posted 1996 net income of $526 million, on net sales of $26 billion, down from 1995 earnings of $916 million on sales of $26.43 billion. GM attributed the decline in earnings to U.S. and Canadian strikes and model changeovers that curtailed production.
Excluding special charges for plant sales and retiree lump-sum, Delphi's 1996 earnings would have been $728 million.

Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. analyst Kenneth Blaschke said the disclosure is a "positive step toward eliminating the conglomerate discount" on GM's stock, which closed up 12.5 cents at $57.75 Tuesday on the New York Stock Exchange.
On Wednesday, GM closed up 12.5 cents at $57.75.

"But it also shows that there is clearly room for improvement at Delphi," Blaschke said. "If (Delphi President) J.T. Battenberg and Losh can reach their goal of increasing non-GM content, Delphi will be a viable global supplier."

The results also showed the performance of GM's North American vehicle profits for the first time excluding Delphi, showing that GM makes a larger net profit margin on parts than it does on cars and trucks.
GM's North American Operations without Delphi posted net income of $730 million in 1996, less than half of the $1.47 billion they earned in 1995.
The net profit margin from GM's vehicle operations was 0.8 percent of sales versus 1.5 percent in 1995, while its net margin on parts was 2 percent in 1996 versus 3.5 percent in 1995.
And excluding NAO special gains from the reversal of a plant closing reserve, the GM North American vehicle operations earned only $333 million in 1996, dropping its net margin to 0.4 percent.
GM has had a longstanding goal of earning a net margin of 5 percent on both vehicles and parts to ensure that it can maintain consistent returns and product spending.
"We are not where we need to be yet for either the component business or the vehicle business," Losh said.
But the results do show that both Delphi and NAO have improved significantly since the early 1990s.

GM said Delphi posted a net loss of $462 million in 1991, a loss of $5.62 billion in 1992 before turning a profit of $717 million. NAO vehicle operations posted losses of $7.62 billion in 1991, a loss of $18.89 billion in 1992 and $1.72 billion in 1993.
Both NAO and Delphi losses in 1992 were affected by massive accounting charges for retiree health care benefits in 1992, including $13.92 billion for NAO and $5.75 billion for Delphi.
During the fourth quarter of 1996, GM said Delphi posted a net loss of $146 million on revenues of $6.14 billion, compared to a fourth-quarter 1995 profit of $192 million on sales of $6.48 billion.

Delphi's 1996 fourth quarter loss includes $202 million in special charges related to plant sales and retiree payments, but Losh attributed lower operating primarily attributable to lost production due to strikes and model changeovers.
NAO vehicle operations earned $27 million in the fourth quarter of 1996 on revenues of $22.5 billion, compared with a year-earlier profit of $414 million on sales of $24.31 billion.
Excluding extraordinary gains of $117 million in the fourth quarter of 1996, NAO lost $117 million from cars and trucks.
